The skill: sounds that change at speed

To let speech flow, English speakers change the sound at the end of a word to match the start of the next one. You do not have to produce these changes; recognising them is what stops fast speech sounding like one long word.

  • /t/, /d/, /n/ + /p/, /b/, /m/ → the first sound moves towards the second: ten boys sounds like tem boys; that man like thap man; ground plan like groum plan.
  • /d/ + /g/ → good girl sounds like goog girl.
  • /s/, /z/ + /ʃ/ → this shop sounds like thish-op; these shops like theesh-ops.

Stage 4 · Sense verbs

See, look, watch; hear, listen; and what follows each one

The meanings are close and the grammar is not. Half the errors at this level are prepositions, and the other half are the difference between noticing and choosing.

1 · Read the explanation.
Verbs of the senses

Noticing versus choosing. See and hear happen to you: you do not decide to do them, and they are rarely used in continuous tenses (I see the plate, not I am seeing the plate). Look at, watch and listen to are things you choose to do, and they are perfectly normal in continuous tenses.

Look at or watch? You look at a thing that is still — a photograph, a label, a plate. You watch something that happens or moves — a film, a chef, a match, people eating crisps. A screen is watched; a picture is looked at.

Prepositions. Look at, gaze at, stare at, glance at, glare at, listen to — all take one. See, hear, watch, notice and observe take a direct object with no preposition at all.

After the verb. Watch / see / hear + object + bare infinitive means you experienced the complete event: I heard him say it. The same verbs + object + -ing means you caught it in progress: I heard him saying it.

Linking verbs. Look, taste, smell, sound and feel can describe a quality, and then they take an adjective: it tastes salty, it looks fresh, that sounds terrible. With like they take a noun: it tastes like seaweed.

Speaking quietly. Whisper uses breath instead of voice; murmur is a low, unclear sound. Both can take a direct object: she whispered my name, he murmured something.

The commonest errors at this level
  • I am seeing a film tonight when watching is meant.
  • Listen the music — listen always needs to.
  • Watch at the screen — watch takes no preposition.
  • It tastes well — use the adjective: it tastes good.
  • Distinguish A and B — use between A and B.

Two things to watch

1 — Still or moving? A still thing is looked at; a moving thing or an event is watched. That one question settles most cases.

2 — The preposition belongs to the verb. Learn listen to, look at and glance at as whole units, and the errors disappear.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Choosing the right sense verb

The situation: you spent ten minutes in a kitchen while a chef prepared a dish, and you were paying attention the whole time.

Step 1 — is it still or happening? Happening, and over a period. So watch, not look at, and not see.

Step 2 — preposition? Watch takes a direct object: I watched the chef, never watched at.

Step 3 — whole event or in progress? If you saw him finish the dish: I watched him finish it. If you only caught part of it: I watched him finishing it.

Step 4 — describing the result. A quality after a sense verb takes an adjective: it looked perfect and tasted salty — not tasted saltily.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Noticing against choosing

The split runs through the whole set. Noticing happens without effort and takes a plain object: I saw the plate · I heard a noise. Choosing to direct your senses takes a preposition: look at the label · listen to the piano. Watch is the odd one: it means following something over time, and it takes a plain object — watch the chef, never watch at.

The look family all take at and differ only in manner: gaze at (steadily, absorbed), stare at (long, often rudely), glance at (very briefly), glare at (angrily). Choosing the wrong one is not a grammar mistake but it changes the picture completely.

What follows see, hear and watch

Two forms, two meanings. A bare infinitive reports the whole event, from beginning to end: I watched him drop the plate — it left his hand and it hit the floor. An -ing form reports something in progress, a slice of it: I watched him dropping plates all evening · I heard somebody shouting upstairs. The same applies to see and hear: I saw her leave (she went) against I saw her leaving (I caught her mid-exit).

Taste and smell work two ways. As ordinary verbs they take an object (I tasted the soup); as linking verbs they describe a quality and take an adjective or like + noun: It tastes salty · It tastes like seaweed — never it tastes salt or it tastes as seaweed.

Finally, telling things apart: distinguish between A and B, or distinguish A from B. Tell works the same way in I cannot tell them apart.

Errors to watch: listen the piano → listen to · watch at the chef → watch the chef · I looked the label → looked at · It tastes salt → tastes salty · distinguish between A from B → one pattern or the other.

A meal, written with four senses

Describe eating something so precisely that a reader could pick it out of a line of five dishes.

The brief

Choose one meal or one dish you remember clearly. Describe the smell, the sound, the look and the texture before you describe the taste, and use the right sense verb every time. The reader should be able to identify the dish without you naming it until the end.

1 · Read the model description.
Model · a dish described in four paragraphs

You smell it from the corner of the street, which is the point: an aroma of hot oil, cumin and something sweet underneath, arriving thirty seconds before you can see where it comes from. By the time I reached the stall I had already decided to buy whatever it was.

The sound is the second thing. The man was working two pans at once, and each time he dropped a new batch in, the oil made a noise you could hear across the road. I stood and watched him for four or five minutes. He glanced at me twice, said nothing, and murmured something to the woman taking the money that made her laugh.

On the plate it looked less impressive than it smelt: eight small brown parcels, slightly uneven, on a piece of paper going transparent at the edges. What you notice is the surface, which is not smooth but rough and blistered. I could hear the crunch before I tasted anything, and I now know from the research that this is half of what I thought the flavour was.

Then the taste, which was salty first, savoury underneath, and faintly sour at the very end, from something in the sauce I could not distinguish from vinegar and probably was not. It tasted like nothing I had eaten at home. They were samsa, from a stall outside the bus station, and I have thought about them for two years.
